text: Every neuron ends by passing its sum through an activation function, and it is fair to ask whether that step is really necessary. It costs computation, it complicates the mathematics, and a network without it would be far easier to analyse. The answer is that without the bend, depth is an illusion, and the particular choice of bend turns out to shape how well a network can learn.

Suppose we stack two layers with no activation between them. The first multiplies by a matrix and adds a bias, the second does the same, and if you multiply out the algebra, the two matrices combine into one matrix and the two biases into one bias. Two linear layers are exactly one linear layer in disguise, and the same is true of a hundred of them, so a network without activations can only ever draw straight boundaries, no matter how deep it is.

The first popular choice was the sigmoid, a smooth S-shaped curve that squeezes any number into the range between zero and one. It was attractive because it looks like a neuron that is either quiet or firing, but its tails are almost flat. Far from zero, changing the input barely changes the output, so the slope there is close to nothing, and as we will see when we study backpropagation, a slope near zero means the learning signal almost disappears. Even at its steepest point, the sigmoid's slope is only a quarter.

The rectified linear unit solved much of this with something almost embarrassingly simple: keep positive numbers as they are, and replace negative numbers with zero. Its slope is exactly one wherever the neuron is active, so the learning signal passes through undiminished, and it is extremely cheap to compute. Its weakness is the flat side. A neuron whose input is negative for every example always outputs zero and receives no learning signal, and such a neuron can stay dead for the rest of training.

A single hinge looks like a very limited tool, but hinges combine beautifully. Add a few ReLUs, each shifted to bend at a different point and each scaled by its own weight, and you can build a tent, then a bump, then a curve that follows almost any shape you like as a chain of straight pieces. This is the real reason activations matter: they give the network corners, and enough corners can trace out a curve.

Language models mostly use smoother relatives of ReLU. The Gaussian error linear unit, or GELU, multiplies its input by the probability that a standard normal random number falls below it. For large positive inputs that probability is close to one, so GELU behaves like ReLU, and for large negative inputs it is close to zero. Only near zero does it differ, where the curve is smooth and dips slightly below the axis. GPT-2 and BERT both use GELU, and many recent models use a gated variant called SwiGLU.

So activations are what make depth worth having, and their shape decides how easily learning signals flow back through a network. Next we ask why many layers of these bends can do more than one very wide layer.
